name: The Bottle of the Ifrit
powers: Held a vast ifrit imprisoned for centuries until a fisherman freed him.
description: The sealed copper bottle cast up in the fisherman's net in the Thousand and One Nights tale of the Fisherman and the Jinni, from which a vast ifrit escaped in a pillar of smoke and, furious at his long imprisonment, threatened to kill the man who had freed him. The fisherman saved himself by doubting that so great a being could fit into so small a vessel, tricking the spirit back through its narrow mouth and sealing the bottle once more. In the tale the jar carries the seal of Solomon, whose name had trapped the ifrit in the deep for hundreds of years, and it is the loss of that power that lets the spirit out. The vessel became the archetype of the bottled-jinn motif in world folklore, echoed in every story of a spirit, demon, or giant confined by a magician's seal and released by the unwary.
source: Thousand and One Nights, The Fisherman and the Jinni

name: Inukshuk
powers: Guides travelers and marks the good hunting ground.
description: The inuksuk, often spelled inukshuk, is a figure of stacked stones built by the Inuit and other Arctic peoples as a landmark in landscapes where trees offer no bearings; the Inuktitut name means 'something that acts in the capacity of a human'. Inuksuit marked travel routes, safe crossings, good hunting and fishing places, food caches and camps, and their shapes could carry messages, from the direction to point to a warning of danger. In northern Alaska the Inupiat built lines of them to herd caribou toward hunters. The human-shaped form is properly an inunnguaq, but the simpler inuksuk on the flag of Nunavut has made the stone figure an emblem of the Arctic and of Canada as a whole. Inuit still build them today, and the pattern appears on the Vancouver Olympics emblem, in art and in jewellery.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Ikenga Shrine Figure
powers: Embodies the owner's personal achievement, strength, and right hand.
description: The ikenga is the carved wooden shrine figure of Igbo men, a seated human form with curving horns, a sword and a carved knife held in its hands, standing on the family altar as the image of its owner's achievement and strength. The figure represents the owner's chi, his personal spirit of accomplishment, and the horned head recalls the ram and the aggressive power of the ancestor-hero; when a man prospered, his ikenga was washed, oiled and given offerings, and when he failed or fell, the figure might be cast away. The right hand, in Igbo thought the hand of action, is honored in the ikenga's upraised arm, and the figure is bound up with the owner's own commitment to strive, the word itself carrying the sense of personal strength. Ikenga are carved in many sizes, from small household figures to great ritual sculptures, and they are among the most recognizable of Igbo arts. They remain in use in the shrine houses of Igboland today.

name: Igil (Tuvan Horsehead Fiddle)
description: Two-stringed bowed fiddle of the Tuvans, its hollow wooden body covered with hide and its neck crowned with a carved horse's head. The igil accompanies khoomei throat singing and Tuvan epic song, evoking the gait and voice of a steppe horse; it is prized across Central Asia and appears in the collection of the Russian Museum of Ethnography. The two strings, traditionally of horsehair, are tuned a fifth apart and played with a bow, the instrument held upright on the knee; the sound is soft and nasal, and players imitate the walk, trot and gallop of the horse with the bow. In Tuva, 2009 was declared the Year of the Igil, and the master player Bady-Dorzhu Ondar was celebrated for carrying the instrument onto the world stage. The fiddle accompanies the long epic recitals, its repeated ostinato supporting the singer's phrases, and it is sometimes said to carry the voice of the horse that bore the hero. Today the igil is taught in Tuvan music schools and performed in ensembles around the world.
material: wooden body, hide soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Alash Ensemble; ar.culture.ru 'Igil'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections
